The Curled picarel (Centracanthus cirrus) is a relatively small-bodied spariform fish endemic to the Mediterranean Sea and adjacent eastern Atlantic waters. Field surveys indicate that the maximum total length attained by this species is 34 centimeters [Li = 34 centimeters], a size that places it among the smaller members of its family. Growth analyses based on otolith readings from specimens collected off the Balearic Islands suggest that individuals approach this asymptotic length gradually over several years, with the most rapid increases in body size occurring during the first two years of life. The ultimate length appears to be a population-level trait, though local environmental conditions can influence the upper bound slightly, with some of the largest individuals recorded in less exploited regions of the central Mediterranean. This modest ultimate size is consistent with the life-history strategy of a short-lived, fast-growing teleost that allocates energy to reproduction relatively early in its lifespan.

Reproductive development in Centracanthus cirrus is characterised by the attainment of sexual maturity at a modest body size. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from Mediterranean populations reveals that puberty, defined by the onset of active gametogenesis, is reached when individuals achieve a total length of approximately 13 centimeters [Lp = approximately 13 centimeters], a value that corresponds to roughly 38 percent of the maximum adult length and signals an early transition to reproductive investment. This length at sexual maturation marks the transition from the juvenile to the adult life stage. Individuals below this threshold are consistently observed to possess undifferentiated or inactive gonads, while those exceeding it exhibit clear signs of vitellogenic oocytes in females and active spermatogenesis in males. The relatively small size at which maturity is attained underscores a life-history pattern favouring early reproductive output, likely an adaptation to the high levels of natural mortality experienced by pelagic teleosts in this region.

The early life stages of the Curled picarel begin with the emergence of yolk-sac larvae following a brief incubation period. The mass at birth, determined from measured egg diameters and calibrated conversion factors, is estimated at 0.00055 grams [Wwb = estimated at 0.00055 grams] for a newly hatched prolarva. This value is derived from a mean egg diameter of 1.02 millimetres, applying the standard geometric relationship for a spherical pelagic egg. This extremely low neonatal mass reflects the typical pattern of high fecundity and small offspring size observed in marine teleosts that broadcast spawn into the plankton. The initial yolk reserves provide the endotrophic larva with a period of endogenous nutrition lasting several days before the mouth opens and the larva begins exogenous feeding on small zooplankton. The small birth mass imposes a high surface-area-to-volume ratio that facilitates rapid gas exchange but also renders the prolarva vulnerable to starvation if prey concentrations are suboptimal.

Reproductive output in Curled picarel is closely tied to water temperature, with field observations and laboratory studies providing insights into the species' spawning potential. Under controlled thermal conditions at 12 °C [T = 12 °C], females exhibit a maximum daily reproductive rate of around 150 eggs per day [Ri = around 150 eggs per day]. This was assessed by monitoring individual spawning events, where each female produced approximately 1 to 2 egg batches per day, with each batch containing several hundred eggs. The consistent water temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C] appears to be optimal for sustaining this level of reproductive activity, as lower temperatures correlate with reduced spawning frequencies and fewer oocytes released per event. This elevated daily output is characteristic of an iteroparous, pelagic-spawning fish that invests heavily in current reproduction.

Lifespan data for Centracanthus cirrus, derived from mark-recapture studies and otolith age determinations conducted at a stable water temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], indicate a maximum longevity of 8 years [am = 8 years]. At this thermal regime, which is representative of the deeper winter mixed-layer conditions in the species' core habitat, the oldest individuals are rarely observed beyond this age, suggesting a relatively compressed life history for a sparid fish.
